narrative: A winter storm moved across northern Illinois during the afternoon of January 1st through the early morning of January 2nd.  Snowfall totals were generally in the 3 to 5 inch range, with some higher totals across far northeast Illinois.  The highest totals included 6.5 inches in Hoffman Estates; 5.8 inches in Palatine; 5.5 inches two miles north of Waukegan; 5.4 inches in Evanston and Woodstock and 5.2 inches in Elgin.  Rockford Airport measured 4.8 inches and Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 4.1 inches.

Freezing drizzle and freezing rain developed across northern Illinois during the early afternoon of January 8th and continued through the late evening.  Roads became slippery and numerous accidents and spin outs occurred.  Ice accumulation amounts at ASOS locations included 0.24 inches at DuPage Airport; 0.18 inches at both Chicago Midway and Aurora Airports; 0.15 inches at Chicago O'Hare and Chicago Executive Airports; 0.10 inch at Rockford Airport and 0.08 inches at Waukegan Airport.

A winter storm moved across northern Illinois from the late evening of January 22nd through the morning of January 23rd.  A band of lake effect snow developed over far eastern Cook and far eastern Will Counties as the snow ended late in the morning of January 23rd.  Snowfall totals generally ranged between 3 to 5 inches.  Rockford Airport measured 2.3 inches and Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 3.7 inches.

Lake effect snow developed over far northeast Illinois including Chicago during the early morning of January 28th and continued into the afternoon.  A band of heavy lake effect snow moved across parts of Cook County producing snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour.  Storm total snowfall amounts included 10.0 inches in Wilmette; 9.0 inches near Evanston and Skokie; 8.0 inches in Jefferson Park; 7.2 inches three miles southwest of Chicago Midway Airport; 7.1 inches in Harwood Heights; 6.0 inches in Lincoln Square and 3.3 inches at Chicago O'Hare Airport.

A winter storm moved across northern Illinois on February 2nd producing heavy snow along and south of a line from Mendota to Aurora to Evanston, where snowfall amounts of 8 to 14 inches occurred.  Snow amounts quickly diminished northwest of this line.  Snowfall rates of 1 to 2 inches per hour were observed in the heaviest snow bands.||The highest storm total snowfall totals included 14.3 inches in Mokena; 13.8 inches two miles northwest of Chicago Heights; 13.0 inches in Paxton, Gibson City and Kankakee; 12.6 inches in Minooka; 12.5 inches in Lansing; 12.0 inches in Pontiac; 11.6 inches in Streator and New Lenox; 11.5 inches in Danforth, Frankfort, Lockport and near Emington; 11.2 inches near Burr Ridge; 11.0 inches in Homewood, Oak Lawn, Oak Forrest, Morris, Bradley, Herscher, Fairbury, Crest Hill, Joliet, Elwood and Braidwood.  Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 5.6 inches and the National Weather Service office in Romeoville measured 10.0 inches.

A winter storm moved across northern Illinois on February 17th producing a period of heavy snow during the afternoon and evening.  Winds were gusting to 30 mph producing widespread blowing and drifting snow.  Numerous traffic accidents were reported.||Snowfall amounts were generally in the 3 to 5 inch range across much of the central and southern Chicago Metro area with amounts quickly decreasing across the northern suburbs.  The highest snowfall totals were generally along and south of Interstate 80.  Some of the highest storm total snowfall amounts included 8.0 inches in Gibson City; 7.0 inches in Strawn; 6.5 inches near Kankakee; 6.0 inches in Streator and near Fairbury; 5.5 inches six miles east of Ashkum; 5.0 inches in Chatsworth and three miles west of Marseilles.  Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 2.9 inches.

Light snow moved across most of northern Illinois during the afternoon of February 24th and transitioned to a mix of light snow and light freezing drizzle and freezing rain for areas south of Interstate 80, in east central Illinois.  These areas received a light glaze of ice accumulation.  Another period of light snow occurred from the evening of February 24th through the early morning of February 25th and mainly for areas along and north of Interstate 80.  Storm total snowfall amounts were generally 1 to 3 inches, except in far northeast Illinois where a localized area of 3 to 5 inches of snow occurred, generally along and north of Interstate 90.

High winds developed across northern Illinois during the afternoon of April 14th producing localized wind damage.  Measured wind gusts include 63 mph near West Brooklyn; 63 mph at the Waukegan Airport; 60 mph near Herbert and near Darien; 59 mph at the Chicago O'Hare and Chicago Midway Airports and 58 mph at DuPage Airport.  A large tree limb was blown down onto a car along Hutchinson Street in the Uptown neighborhood of Chicago.  An 8 inch diameter tree was uprooted in Herrick Lake Forest Preserve near Warrenville Road and a section of a fence was also blown down nearby. A tree fell blocking Portwine Road, north of Deerfield Road in Riverwoods.  A semi truck was blown over along Interstate 55 near Pontiac.

A supercell thunderstorm moved across northeast Illinois including Chicago and the western suburbs during the late afternoon and early evening of June 13th.  Widespread significant wind damage occurred in many areas and two tornadoes occurred.  Thousands of trees were damaged and hundreds of trees were snapped or uprooted.  Several houses were damaged, some significantly, by falling trees.  Numerous vehicles were damaged or crushed by falling trees or tree limbs.

Hot and humid conditions developed across most of northern Illinois during the afternoon of July 5th.  High temperatures were in the mid 90s and afternoon peak heat indices were in the 105 to 110 degree range. Temperatures and heat indices were cooler across far northeast Illinois and near Lake Michigan.

A man went swimming in Lake Michigan during the evening of July 13th near Jarvis Beach in Chicago.  He was pinned against a break wall by large waves.  Three of his friends used a nearby life ring which they threw to him and were able to help pull him to shore.  Red do not swim flags were flying at the beach and the group had been warned not to enter the water by lifeguards who had just left for the day.  Waves at the nearby Wilmette buoy were 3 to 4 feet and had peaked around 5 feet a few hours earlier.  ||In a separate incident about 24 hours later, on the evening of July 14th, a 14 year old boy was pulled from Lake Michigan at North Avenue Beach in Chicago.  He was taken to a hospital in serious condition.  Waves at the Wilmette Buoy were 2 to 3 feet with northeast wind directions all day.

An arctic cold front moved across northern Illinois during the late morning and afternoon of December 22nd.  Temperatures fell from the lower to middle 30s into the single digits within hours.  Snow quickly spread across the region with roads becoming snow covered.  The snow tapered off to snow showers in the evening and snow showers continued through the afternoon of December 23rd.  Total snowfall amounts were generally in the 1 to 3 inch range with an area of 3 to 5 inches across far northwest Illinois.  Winds gusted as high as 55 mph through the morning of December 23rd and continued gusting to 40 mph through that evening producing widespread blowing snow and near whiteout conditions in many areas, especially in rural and open areas.

An arctic cold front moved across northern Illinois during the late morning and afternoon of December 22nd.  Temperatures were in the lower to middle 30s ahead of the front and fell into the single digits within hours after the cold front passed.  Low temperatures by the morning of December 23rd ranged from 5 below to 12 below zero.  High temperatures on December 23rd remained in the low single digits below zero.  Winds gusted as high as 55 mph through the morning of December 23rd and continued gusting to 40 mph through the evening of December 23rd.  The combination of strong winds and sub zero temperatures produced wind chills between 30 below and 42 below zero.  While temperatures slowly warmed to near zero by the morning of December 24th, winds continued gusting to 35 mph.  Wind chills finally warmed above 20 below zero by the late morning of December 24th.

From the morning of January 28th through late that night, a winter storm brought impactful snow and freezing rain to parts of northern Illinois. Rain and snow began moving into the area during the predawn hours of the 28th and continued into the overnight with the heaviest snow falling during the afternoon and evening. The hardest-hit areas wound up with 5 to 8 inches of snow in extreme northern and northeastern Illinois and up to a tenth of an inch of ice accumulation across portions of the Chicago metropolitan area. Both the snow and ice made for hazardous travel conditions with local media reporting several automobile accidents as a result. A winter weather advisory had been issued for most of the CWA with the area's northern-most counties later upgraded to a winter storm warning prior to the event. O'Hare Airport measured 2.3 inches of snow and 0.04 inches of ice accumulation. Rockford Airport measured 5.1 inches of snow.

Snow developed across far northern Illinois during the morning of February 16th and continued into the late evening.  The snow was heavy at times with a band of 3 to 5 inches across far northern Illinois and a band of 5 to 8 inches of snow across far northwest Illinois.  The highest storm total snowfall amounts included 7.0 inches in Roscoe; 6.8 inches in Rockton; 5.6 inches four miles north northwest of Rockford and 3.6 inches at the Rockford Airport.||A wintry mix developed south of the snow generally between Interstates 88 and 80 where light freezing rain occurred during the day and then a period of snow occurred in the evening.  Measured ice accumulations included 0.25 inches at Sugar Grove Airport; 0.10 inches at DuPage Airport; 0.06 inches at Chicago O'Hare Airport; 0.03 inches at Chicago Executive Airport in Wheeling and 0.02 inches at Chicago Midway Airport.||Winds were gusting as high as 45 mph and a tree was blown down, falling on four  pedestrians on the Northwestern University Campus in Evanston.  Three were transported to a hospital with injuries, one with a serious head injury.  The fourth was treated at the scene.

Scattered thunderstorms moved across northern Illinois during the morning of February 27th producing three tornadoes and isolated wind damage.  High winds developed during the evening of February 27th resulting in isolated wind damage in Chicago where a large tree fell onto two homes in the 1700 block of 101st Street in the Beverly neighborhood of Chicago.  Both homes suffered structural damage.  A 48 year old man was taken to the hospital in good condition, though what his injuries were and how they occurred were unknown.

During the afternoon and evening of the 31st, a wave of severe thunderstorms produced numerous tornadoes, severe hail, extensive wind damage, and localized flooding across northern and northeastern Illinois. A total of 37 tornadoes were confirmed across the state. The NWS Chicago office tied a record for the most tornadoes to occur in a single calendar day within the office's county warning area with 22, 17 of which occurred in Illinois. One EF-2 tornado occurred in south-central Lee County and two others in northwest Indiana. Some of the more notable damage includes multiple semi trucks blown over, a garage that had been completely destroyed southeast of Amboy, and the partial roof collapse of the Apollo Theatre in Belvidere which unfortunately resulted in one fatality and 40 injuries.

Severe drought conditions developed rapidly across northeast Illinois during the middle of June, which was referred to as a flash drought.  Precipitation amounts were well below normal.  For the month of June, Rockford Airport measured 1.90 inches, which was 3.33 inches below normal.  Aurora Airport measured 1.03 inches, which was 2.95 inches below normal. DuPage Airport measured 1.17 inches which was 2.48 inches below normal. The National Weather Service office in Romeoville measured 1.20 inches, which was 3.48 inches below normal. Waukegan Airport measured 1.72 inches, which was 2.73 inches below normal. Chicago Executive Airport measured 1.69 inches, which was 2.28 inches below normal. Chicago Midway Airport measured 2.08 inches, which was 1.93 inches below normal. Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 2.36 inches which was 1.74 inches below normal.  Many creeks, streams and rivers were running well below their normal long term averages by the end of June.

An abnormally dry start to summer 2023 carried over into July with the majority of the CWA entering the month in a severe drought. However, several noteworthy rain events throughout the month brought a good deal of relief to much of the area. By the end of the month, only a sliver of the CWA remained in a severe drought while elsewhere had improved.

An extreme rainfall event occurred on July 2 in the Chicago metropolitan area caused by multiple nearly stationary bands of showers and thunderstorms near a slow-moving low pressure area. Rainfall occurred over from approximately 12 AM CST to 6 PM CST, with peak rainfall rates exceeding 2 inches per hour and storm total accumulations nearing 9.0 inches in Cook County. Individual showers and thunderstorms moved very slowly during the event, with storm motions of 15 mph or less, leading to extended periods of heavy rainfall. The area of peak rainfall just west of Chicago was estimated to have less than a 1% chance of occurring annually, and led to widespread flooding of basements, streets, and expressways. Also happening on this day was the first annual NASCAR Chicago street race downtown. The storm temporarily flooded portions of the race course, caused a number of delays and cancellations of events, and made conditions terribly slick for the drivers on the course.

Several rain gauges around the area recorded one to two inches of rain within a 30 minute period underneath some of these storms. The city of Chicago and its near-south and near-west suburbs were the areas hit hardest. Numerous reports were received of flooded roads, including a number of residential streets. Additionally, two firefighters were injured battling a fire caused by lightning striking a townhouse.

A series of thunderstorms brought torrential rainfall and widespread flooding to much of the Chicago metro area, namely the south and west suburbs and up into the city of Chicago. Several Oswego District 308 schools received water and storm damage. Flood damages were estimated at around $288 million across the metro area, most of which came from the city of Chicago which alone accounted for roughly $230 million in damages with roughly 40,000 individual structures flooded around the city. The remainder of Cook County accounted for roughly $57 million in flood damages with more than 10,000 additional structures flooded. Several instances of wind damage were also reported, mostly damage to trees.

During the afternoon and evening of the 18th, a few rounds of thunderstorms brought torrential rainfall to much of northern Illinois resulting in flash flooding. One particularly strong storm also produced damaging winds in DeKalb County. Initial reports estimate $8.8 million in flood damages around northern and northeast Illinois, and around $2.5 million in the city of Chicago alone.

High winds produced localized wind damage during the afternoon of October 21st across northeast Illinois.  A tree was blown down onto power lines that were blocking a road in Glen Ellyn.  A tree was blown down at the corner of Kedvale Avenue and Pratt Avenue in Lincolnwood.

Heavy lake effect snow fell on parts of northeastern Illinois as a compact system of low pressure moved east of Lake Michigan on the 9th and into the morning of the 10th. The most snow fell in northeastern Lake County as well as north-central Iroquois into eastern Kankakee counties. Reports of 6 to 10 inches came out of Lake County. In Iroquois and Kankakee counties, as many as 9 to 12 inches fell in the course of about six hours. The city of Chicago was gapped by the higher accumulations with O'Hare Airport having received 1.7 inches in total.

Late during the night of the 25th into the following morning on the 26th, strong wind gusts overspread northern Illinois as a large winter storm departed the region. A Wind Advisory was in effect across the area.

A significant winter storm impacted a large stretch of the Midwest during the night of the 28th and through the night of the 29th. Multiple rounds of moderate to occasionally heavy snow fell on the area throughout the day. Widespread snow totals in the 6 to 9 inch range were observed across northern Illinois. The highest totals were observed north of I-80 with some isolated accumulations near 1 foot near the Wisconsin state line.

A period of light snow spread across all of northern Illinois during the afternoon of December 1st and continued through the late evening, affecting the afternoon commute.  Snowfall amounts were generally 1 to 3 inches for areas north of Interstate 80 and 2 to 4 inches for areas along and south of Interstate 80.

Snow began across northern Illinois during the late evening of December 6th and continued into the morning of December 7th. A large swath of 5 to 7 inches fell along and north of a Dixon to Evanston line with 3 to 5 inches falling south of this line to Interstate 80.  Rockford Airport measured 5.8 inches and Chicago O'Hare Airport measured 4.8 inches.

Bitterly cold air moved across Illinois during mid December with wind chills 20 below to 25 below zero for many areas with a few locations as low as 30 below zero on the morning of December 14th.  Wind chills were 20 below to 25 below zero across central Illinois on the morning of December 15th.

Strong winds and periods of snow caused significant blowing snow across much of northern Illinois from early morning through early afternoon on December 29th.  Visibilities were frequently under one mile, especially in rural areas.  Winds were frequently gusting between 40 mph and 50 mph with higher peak gusts, including a gust to 60 mph at the Sugar Grove Airport.
